svg.title: The signed-clock stall of the camp wait
svg.desc: The camp wait compares stamp + $14 with the sim clock word $2df72 as signed words, so a group camped before tick 32768 waits about 34,800 ticks once the clock passes 32768. Sources (reversing/powermonger/strategy.md): "Where it runs" (the $13000 listing: $1302e addq.l #1,$2df70), "The commander AI `$6522`" bullet "The signed-clock stall" (mechanism, W5G_k80 / W5G_k108 chunks: 1500 and 1843 decisions per chunk, 168 / 93 in the crossing chunk, 0 after; clock 32599 / 32674; stamps 2088 / 2038), "Isolation by clock pokes" (the five-row table, start L2G_k80_c8.snap, clock 11729, stamp 2088, stamp + 20 = 2108, about 167k steps per tick), "$51538 group-order table" (word 256 stamped by $3720). Literal scans of scratchpad/pm123/win/m1_map.ram $0..$40000: $2df72 in the instructions at $3720 and $65a0 only; the long $2df70 at $12f6 and $1352 (copies to $2df74), $1302e (increment), $1373c (compare with $2df74), $13baa (clr.l). LOAD note: strategy.md "The loaded camp stamps against the kept clock" and the stall bullet "A LOAD is a second way into the stall" (py/saveload/camp_stamps.py). Full fact list: clock_stall.facts.md.
svg.text: A 16-bit clock bug stops the computer's idle armies deciding for about 34,800 ticks
The camp wait compares tick numbers as signed 16-bit words, so after tick 32768 a group stamped earlier looks as if it camped in the future
proven (checked against the game's own code)
observed (seen in the running game)
inferred (read from the code, not run)
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990, here the Atari ST version) is a war game in which the computer lords command armies
through captains' groups. This figure comes from reverse-engineering the game's 68000 machine code (the ST's CPU) and running it in an
emulator. The lords' commander AI ($6522) runs once per tick, the game's simulation step, and offers each group an order. A group that
has just gone back to camp (the state it waits in for its next order) is held for 20 ticks first: the game stores the tick at which it
camped (its camp stamp) and waits while stamp + 20 is greater than the current tick.
The bug: both numbers are 16-bit words and the compare is signed. Once the tick count passes 32768 the clock word reads as a negative
number, so every group stamped before then looks as if it camped in the future and waits about 34,800 more ticks, until the clock wraps
past 65536 and climbs back to its stamp. In a long game the computer's camped armies stop deciding. Panel A shows the code, B the
arithmetic, C the experiment that proves the cause, D the stall in untouched play.
$ numbers are addresses in the game's memory, given as citations; the text says what each one is. Evidence: proven = checked against the game's own code
with a match count; observed = seen in the running game; inferred = read from the code or reasoned, not run.

g.text: the 32-bit clock; $2df72 is its low word
as the group goes back to camp

svg.text: How to read: the three pieces of code that touch the clock word ($2df72). Left: the tick adds one to the 32-bit clock, whose low word is $2df72.
Middle: a group going back to camp copies that word into its record as its camp stamp. Right: the wait test. bgt is the 68000's signed "branch if
greater", so a clock word of 32768 or more is read as negative. A scan of the game's code for the literal $2df72 finds it in these two instructions
only (the only place the word is read).

g.text: B. One camped group, stamped at tick 2088: the clock in ticks since the land (the game map) was built
At tick 34104 the word reads -31432 and 2108 > -31432, so the group waits. Groups that re-camp every few ticks (stamps within 20 ticks
of the clock; two lands tested) do not stall. Instructions ("steps") per tick differ per land, so the crossing is at a different step count.

svg.text: How to read: a number line of the clock in ticks since the land was built, with the signed value the compare sees underneath. The group camped at
tick 2088, so from tick 2108 it may decide (green). At 32768 the signed value jumps to -32768, 2108 is now "greater" than the clock, and the group
waits (grey) until the clock wraps and reaches 65536 + 2108.

g.text: C. Experiment: set the clock by hand, one value per run, from one saved game (clock 11729; about 167k steps per tick)
crosses 32768 at tick 16; last hit 2,346,222, then none
same write, no crossing in the budget: same as no change
below 2108: waits about 60 ticks; first hit 9,711,010
waits until the clock reaches 2108: about 2140 ticks
Each prediction was written before its run; 5 of 5 met. With $7ff0 the AI routine itself still runs (604 hits against 599): only the compare gates decisions.

svg.text: How to read: one row per run. Every run starts from the same saved game state, writes one value into the clock word and nothing else, and counts how
often the decision point ($65b4, the first instruction after the compare) is reached. The bar is steps after the change: green where decisions
happen, grey where the group waits. A step is one emulated 68000 instruction; M is a million, G a thousand million.
Takeaway: changing only the clock word switches the decisions off and on exactly where the signed compare predicts, and the AI routine itself keeps
running, so the compare is the cause.

g.text: D. In normal play: two lands left untouched for 7G steps, decisions counted per 250M-step chunk
0 in chunks 12 to 20 (crossing chunk ends at clock 32674)
Bars are run counts; the pre-crossing rate is drawn flat from the one figure the doc gives. Chunk n spans 2G + (n-1) x 250M to 2G + n x 250M.

svg.text: How to read: two lands (land A and land B) built with the game's Play Random Land option and left to play with no input for 7G steps. Each bar
segment is one 250M-step chunk; the number is how often $65b4 (the decision point) was reached in it. The short segment is the chunk in which the
clock passes 32768.
Takeaway: in untouched play the decisions stop within one chunk, at a different step count per land, because a tick costs a different number of steps
on each land.

g.text: Status: the compare is the cause in the emulator (proven by panel C). The same stall on a real ST or in Hatari is inferred from the code, not run.
Consequence: past 4.5G to 5.75G steps a natural run loses its idle camped groups' decisions for about 6G steps; "no late decisions" is not "unreachable".
Second route into the wait: a LOAD restores the saved camp stamps but keeps the running game's clock, so a stamp can be ahead of the clock.
One predicted run (a saved land loaded at clock 441, stamp 2088): first decision predicted at clock 2108, about 279.2M steps;
observed at clock 2108 after 276,745,802 steps (0.9% early). Proven by prediction.

svg.text: Terms and evidence
Proven: checked in the emulator by an experiment whose outcome was predicted before it ran (panel C, 5 of 5 predictions met; the LOAD route, one
prediction). Observed: seen running in the emulator and counted. Inferred: read from the code and not run; here, that a real ST or the Hatari
emulator (another ST emulator) stalls the same way, since the code is the game's own. 256(A1) is the camp stamp word of the group the AI loop is
looking at.
Sources: strategy.md "The signed-clock stall", "Isolation by clock pokes", "$51538 group-order table"; saved game L2G_k80_c8.snap (panel C); runs W5G_k108 (land A) and W5G_k80 (land
B), py/arms/batch4.sh (panel D); lo.st loaded into rand1, py/saveload/camp_stamps.py (LOAD route); literal scan py/find_field_writers.py; clock_stall.facts.md.
